title: Marie Curie: Radioactivity Pioneer
description: Barrier-breaking science in an age of discovery and risk.

questions.question: Who became the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, sharing the 1903 physics prize?
questions.explanation: The original nomination named only Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel. Pierre wrote that he wished to be considered together with Marie, and she shared the prize.

questions.question: In 1898, Marie Curie named her first new element after which country—one that had been wiped off the map?
questions.explanation: Polonium was a protest. Poland had been carved up by Russia, Prussia, and Austria, and wouldn't be independent again until 1918. Curie grew up in Russian-ruled Warsaw.

questions.question: Months after naming polonium for Poland, the Curies announced a second element that glowed in the dark. What was it?
questions.explanation: Purifying a tenth of a gram took nearly four years and about a ton of pitchblende in a leaky shed. At night she and Pierre slipped back in just to watch the tubes glow.

questions.question: When radium won her a second Nobel in 1911, she was urged to skip the ceremony over a scandal involving which physicist?
questions.explanation: Newspapers exposed her affair with the married Langevin, and a Nobel committee member asked her not to come. She replied that science and private life were unrelated, and went.

questions.question: Three years after the Langevin uproar, war broke out—and she drove mobile X-ray units to the front, nicknamed what?
questions.explanation: The Academy of Sciences had rejected her in 1911; France still needed her. She equipped about 20 vans and 200 field posts, learned to drive, and worked beside her 17-year-old daughter Irène.

deeperMode.title: The Deadly Glow
deeperMode.description: The human cost of chasing unknown rays

questions.question: Curie's notebooks are still too radioactive to handle unprotected. In what kind of boxes does France keep them?
questions.hint: A heavy gray metal that blocks radiation

questions.question: What ultimately caused Marie Curie's death, likely from years of radiation exposure?
questions.hint: A blood disorder where the bone marrow stops producing enough blood cells
